los.text: Describe the main signs, symptoms and causes of common endocrine disorders (thyroxine, cortisol, parathyroid hormone, anti-diuretic hormone, growth hormone, prolactin)
los.html:
HormoneExcessDeficiency
ThyroxineHyperthyroidism (Graves', toxic nodule): weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations/AF, anxiety, diarrhoeaHypothyroidism (Hashimoto's): weight gain, cold intolerance, fatigue, constipation, bradycardia, dry skin, menorrhagia, slow-relaxing reflexes
CortisolCushing's: central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple striae, proximal myopathy, bruising, HTN, diabetes, osteoporosisAddison's: fatigue, weight loss, pigmentation (primary), postural hypotension, ↓Na⁺ ↑K⁺, hypoglycaemia; crisis = shock
PTHPrimary hyperparathyroidism (adenoma): hypercalcaemia "bones, stones, abdominal groans, psychic moans", polyuriaHypoparathyroidism (post-thyroidectomy): hypocalcaemia: perioral tingling, tetany, Chvostek/Trousseau, long QT, seizures
ADHSIADH (lung cancer, CNS disease, drugs: SSRIs, carbamazepine): euvolaemic hyponatraemiaDiabetes insipidus (cranial: trauma, tumour; nephrogenic: lithium, ↑Ca²⁺): polyuria, polydipsia, dilute urine, hypernatraemia
GHAcromegaly (adults: large hands/feet, coarse face, prognathism, sweating, carpal tunnel, diabetes, HTN) / gigantism (children)Short stature in children; ↓ muscle mass, ↑ fat, fatigue in adults
ProlactinProlactinoma, drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide), hypothyroidism: galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, infertility, ↓ libido, erectile dysfunctionFailure of lactation (Sheehan's syndrome after PPH)
  • Pituitary tumours also cause mass effects: headache, bitemporal hemianopia (optic chiasm), cranial nerve palsies (cavernous sinus).

los.text: Describe the causes, investigations, diagnosis and principles of treatment and management of thyroid disease (hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, thyroid nodules)
los.html:
• Ix: TSH first (most sensitive), then free T4 (± free T3).
    • Antibodies: TPO (Hashimoto's), TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) (Graves').
    • Thyroid USS for nodules
    • radionuclide uptake scan (Graves' diffuse ↑, toxic nodule hot, thyroiditis ↓).
PatternInterpretation
↑TSH, ↓T4Primary hypothyroidism
↑TSH, normal T4Subclinical hypothyroidism
↓TSH, ↑T4/T3Primary hyperthyroidism
↓TSH, ↓T4Secondary (pituitary) hypothyroidism or sick euthyroid
Hypothyroidism
  • Causes: Hashimoto's (commonest in UK), post-radioiodine/surgery, drugs (amiodarone, lithium), iodine deficiency (worldwide).
  • Rx: levothyroxine (start 50–100 μg; 25 μg if elderly/IHD), titrate to TSH every 6–8 weeks
  • Increase dose in pregnancy.
  • Myxoedema coma: IV liothyronine + hydrocortisone.
Hyperthyroidism
  • Causes: Graves' (eye disease, pretibial myxoedema, diffuse goitre, bruit)
  • Toxic multinodular goitre
  • Toxic adenoma
  • Thyroiditis (de Quervain's painful, postpartum: self-limiting, no antithyroid drugs)
  • Amiodarone.
  • Rx: β-blocker (propranolol) for symptoms
  • Carbimazole (block-and-titrate or block-and-replace, 12–18 months; agranulocytosis → stop if sore throat, check FBC; PTU in 1st trimester, hepatotoxic)
  • Radioiodine (contraindicated in pregnancy/active eye disease)
  • Thyroidectomy.
  • Thyroid storm: emergency.
Thyroid nodules
  • Common
  • Most benign.
  • Assess with TFTs + USS (U-grading) → FNA cytology (Thy/Bethesda) if suspicious.
  • Red flags: rapidly growing, hard/fixed, hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve), stridor, lymphadenopathy, childhood neck radiation → 2WW.
  • Cancers: papillary (commonest, lymphatic spread, good prognosis), follicular (haematogenous), medullary (calcitonin, MEN2), anaplastic (elderly, aggressive).

los.text: Describe the causes, investigations, diagnosis and principles of treatment and management of Cushing syndrome and adrenal insufficiency
sessions: Clin 3: Cushing's syndrome and adrenal insufficiency
los.html:
Cushing's syndrome

Causes
  • Exogenous steroids (commonest)
  • ACTH-dependent: pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease, ~70% of endogenous), ectopic ACTH (small cell lung cancer: hypokalaemia, pigmentation, rapid onset)
  • ACTH-independent: adrenal adenoma/carcinoma.
Screening tests(need 1–2)Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test (failure to suppress morning cortisol), late-night salivary cortisol, 24 h urinary free cortisol.
Localisation
  • Plasma ACTH (low = adrenal; high = pituitary/ectopic) → high-dose dex suppression / CRH test / inferior petrosal sinus sampling
  • MRI pituitary, CT adrenals/chest.
RxTaper exogenous steroids; transsphenoidal surgery; adrenalectomy; resect ectopic source; medical (metyrapone, ketoconazole, osilodrostat).

Adrenal insufficiency

Primary (Addison's)Autoimmune (UK commonest), TB (worldwide), metastases, haemorrhage (Waterhouse–Friderichsen). ↓ cortisol and ↓ aldosterone → ↓Na⁺, ↑K⁺, hypotension, pigmentation (↑ ACTH/MSH).
SecondaryPituitary disease or sudden withdrawal of long-term steroids (commonest overall); no hyperkalaemia or pigmentation (aldosterone preserved).
Ix9am cortisol (low); short Synacthen test (failure of cortisol to rise after ACTH); ACTH level; renin/aldosterone; adrenal antibodies.
Rx
  • Hydrocortisone (2–3 daily doses) + fludrocortisone (primary)
  • Sick day rules (double oral dose when febrile; IM hydrocortisone if vomiting), steroid emergency card, medical alert.
Adrenal crisis (shock, vomiting, hyponatraemia): IV/IM hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately + IV 0.9% saline (and glucose). Don't wait for test results.

los.text: Describe the causes, investigations, diagnosis and principles of treatment and management of disorders of calcium / phosphate metabolism and the parathyroid gland
sessions: Clin 4: Disorders of parathyroid gland and calcium/phosphate metabolism
los.html:
Hypercalcaemia

Causes
  • Primary hyperparathyroidism (↑Ca, ↑/inappropriately normal PTH, ↓PO₄; parathyroid adenoma ~85%) and malignancy (↓PTH: PTHrP from squamous cancers, bone metastases, myeloma) = 90%.
  • Others: thiazides, lithium, vitamin D excess, sarcoidosis, immobilisation, FHH (low urine Ca), tertiary hyperparathyroidism (CKD).
SymptomsThirst/polyuria, renal stones, abdominal pain, constipation, pancreatitis, PUD, bone pain/osteoporosis, confusion, depression, short QT.
Acute Rx(Ca >3.0 or symptomatic)IV 0.9% saline rehydration (3–4 L/day), then IV bisphosphonate (zoledronate/pamidronate); treat cause. Calcitonin, steroids (sarcoid, lymphoma), denosumab.
Primary HPT RxParathyroidectomy if symptomatic, Ca >2.85, renal stones/↓ eGFR, osteoporosis, age <50; cinacalcet if unfit.

Hypocalcaemia

Causes
  • Vitamin D deficiency
  • CKD (↓ 1α-hydroxylation, ↑ PO₄)
  • Hypoparathyroidism (post-thyroid/parathyroid surgery, autoimmune, DiGeorge)
  • Hypomagnesaemia (↓ PTH release and action)
  • Pancreatitis
  • Massive transfusion
  • Pseudohypoparathyroidism (PTH resistance).
Correct for albuminCorrected Ca = total Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin).
Rx
  • Severe/symptomatic → IV calcium gluconate 10% (ECG monitoring)
  • Oral calcium + vitamin D (colecalciferol; alfacalcidol/calcitriol in CKD or hypoparathyroidism)
  • Correct Mg²⁺.

Phosphate

  • ↑ PO₄: CKD, hypoparathyroidism, tumour lysis, rhabdomyolysis. ↓ PO₄: refeeding syndrome, vitamin D deficiency, hyperparathyroidism, alcoholism, DKA treatment.

los.text: Describe the roles of parathyroid hormone and vitamin D in controlling calcium and phosphate homeostasis in health
sessions: BMS 1: Calcium, vitamin D and PTH
los.html:
Calcium
  • ~99% in bone
  • Plasma total 2.2–2.6 mmol/L: ~45% ionised (active), ~45% protein-bound (albumin), ~10% complexed.
  • Alkalosis ↑ binding → ↓ ionised Ca (tingling with hyperventilation).
PTH(chief cells; released when ionised Ca²⁺ falls, sensed by calcium-sensing receptor; needs Mg²⁺)
  • Bone: ↑ resorption (via osteoblast RANKL → osteoclasts) → releases Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻.
  • Kidney: ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption (DCT), ↓ phosphate reabsorption (PCT, phosphaturia), ↑ 1α-hydroxylase → calcitriol.
  • Gut (indirect via calcitriol).
  • Net: ↑ Ca²⁺, ↓ PO₄³⁻.
Vitamin D
  • Skin (UVB on 7-dehydrocholesterol → cholecalciferol D3) or diet (D2/D3)
  • → liver 25-hydroxylation
  • → 25(OH)D (storage form, measured)
  • → kidney 1α-hydroxylation (↑ by PTH, ↓ PO₄; ↓ by FGF23)
  • → 1,25(OH)₂D (calcitriol): ↑ gut absorption of Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻, bone mineralisation (and resorption at high levels), feedback ↓ PTH.
FGF23(osteocytes)↑ phosphate excretion, ↓ calcitriol.
Calcitonin(thyroid C cells)↓ osteoclast activity; minor role in humans (tumour marker for medullary thyroid cancer).
DeficiencyRickets (children), osteomalacia (adults: bone pain, proximal myopathy, ↓Ca, ↓PO₄, ↑ALP, ↑PTH).

los.text: Describe the regulation and effects of thyroxine in health
los.html:
Regulation (HPT axis)Hypothalamic TRH → anterior pituitary TSH → thyroid follicular cells. Negative feedback of T4/T3 on hypothalamus and pituitary.
Synthesis
  • Iodide trapped by Na⁺/I⁻ symporter (NIS)
  • → oxidised by thyroid peroxidase (TPO)
  • → iodinates tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin (MIT, DIT)
  • → coupling (T4 = DIT + DIT; T3 = MIT + DIT)
  • → stored in colloid
  • → endocytosis and proteolysis
  • → release.
  • Thyroid secretes mostly T4 (~90%)
  • T3 is the active form (5′-deiodinase converts T4 → T3 in tissues; also → inactive reverse T3 in illness).
Transport>99% protein-bound (TBG, transthyretin, albumin); only free hormone is active (↑ TBG in pregnancy/oestrogen → total T4 ↑, free normal).
MechanismLipid-soluble → nuclear thyroid hormone receptors → gene transcription.
Effects
  • ↑ basal metabolic rate (↑ Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, O₂ consumption, heat)
  • ↑ β-adrenergic receptor expression (↑ HR, contractility: CO)
  • ↑ gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, protein turnover
  • Essential for CNS development and growth in fetus/children (congenital hypothyroidism → cretinism; screened by heel prick)
  • Bone growth (with GH)
  • ↑ gut motility
  • Reflexes.
DrugsCarbimazole/PTU (block TPO), amiodarone and lithium (dysfunction), iodine (Wolff–Chaikoff effect).

los.text: Explain the effects and regulation of hormones secreted from the adrenal gland (adrenaline, aldosterone, cortisol, androgens) in health
los.html:
• Adrenal cortex zones ("GFR → salt, sugar, sex"):
ZoneHormoneRegulationEffects
GlomerulosaAldosterone (mineralocorticoid)Angiotensin II, ↑K⁺ (ACTH minor)↑ Na⁺ reabsorption + K⁺ and H⁺ excretion in collecting duct (ENaC, Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) → ↑ BP/volume
FasciculataCortisol (glucocorticoid)CRH → ACTH; diurnal rhythm (peak ~8am), stress
  • ↑ gluconeogenesis, ↑ protein catabolism, lipolysis (central fat redistribution), insulin resistance
  • Anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive
  • Permissive for catecholamines (↑ BP)
  • ↓ bone formation
  • Mood effects
ReticularisAndrogens (DHEA, androstenedione)ACTHPubic/axillary hair (adrenarche), libido in women; excess → hirsutism, virilisation (CAH)
Adrenal medulla(chromaffin cells, modified sympathetic ganglion)
  • Adrenaline (~80%) and noradrenaline, released on sympathetic preganglionic (ACh, nicotinic) stimulation.
  • Cortisol from the cortex (portal flow) induces PNMT (NA → adrenaline).
  • Effects: fight or flight: ↑ HR/contractility, glycogenolysis, lipolysis, bronchodilation, redistribution of blood flow.
DisordersConn's (↑ aldosterone: HTN + hypokalaemia), CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency), phaeochromocytoma (episodic HTN, headache, sweating, palpitations).

los.text: Describe the regulation and effects of growth hormone in health
los.html:
Regulation
  • Hypothalamic GHRH (+) and somatostatin (−)
  • Pulsatile release, largest during deep (slow-wave) sleep.
  • Stimulated by ghrelin, hypoglycaemia, fasting, exercise, stress, amino acids (arginine), puberty (sex steroids).
  • Inhibited by hyperglycaemia, IGF-1 (negative feedback), somatostatin, obesity, glucocorticoids.
MechanismGH receptor → JAK2–STAT signalling.
Direct effects(anti-insulin, metabolic)↑ lipolysis, ↓ glucose uptake/↑ hepatic glucose output (diabetogenic), ↑ protein synthesis.
Indirect effects via IGF-1(liver; also locally)Linear growth (chondrocyte proliferation at epiphyseal growth plates), muscle and organ growth, protein synthesis.
Life stagesEssential for childhood growth (with thyroid hormone, sex steroids in puberty); in adults maintains body composition, bone density, well-being.
Testing
  • Random GH is unhelpful (pulsatile).
  • Excess → measure IGF-1, confirm with OGTT (GH fails to suppress).
  • Deficiency → stimulation tests (insulin tolerance test, glucagon, GHRH–arginine).
TreatmentAcromegaly → transsphenoidal surgery, somatostatin analogues (octreotide), pegvisomant (GH receptor antagonist); deficiency → recombinant GH (somatropin).
